newsitem.title: UK: Lower PSBR, axed ACT a double bonus for UK gilts.
newsitem.headline: Lower PSBR, axed ACT a double bonus for UK gilts.

text.p: As the budget dust settles and knee-jerk fears of higher interest rates give way to more considered analysis, economists have come to the conclusion that UK gilt investors have much to be happy about.
They acknowledge that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's failure to restrain booming consumer spending will lead to higher interest rates.

But balanced against that, the sharp falls Brown forecast for Britain's public debt mean the gilt market will have to absorb a minimal amount of new supply, while the abolition of tax credits on Advance Corporation Tax could push institutional investors away from equities, into the arms of the bond market.

Kevin Adams, gilts strategist at BZW, said monetary policy will have to take up the burden of restraining consumer demand, which is getting a huge one-off boost as more than 30 billion pounds in free shares are handed out by building societies which convert into banks.

Economists are talking about base rates, now at 6.5 percent, rising to 7.5 or even eight percent as the Bank of England, now free to set rates, struggles to ward off the inflationary threat of a high street boom.

But higher rates will only savage the short end of the gilt market. Longer-dated bonds should escape pretty much unscathed on the basis that the longer-term inflationary outlook is in safe hands with the Bank.
Adams forecasts short rates will rise by 75 basis points by the end of the year but ultra-long yields will only climb by 25 basis points.
The September gilt future stood at 114-29 midway through Friday's session, about a full point above the low point it hit straight after Brown's budget speech on Wednesday.

Analysts at HSBC Markets agreed the outlook for gilts should be a sunny one. "Once it has recovered from its immediate worries about consumer spending and interest rate prospects, the gilt market may yet rally strongly."

They said the 5.5 billion pounds of fiscal tightening that Brown introduced, and the fact that monetary policy rests with an effectively independent central bank, made a gilt/Bund spread of 153 basis points on Friday, entirely unjustified.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's UK economists, like BZW, forecast curve flattening. "Certainly the curve should flatten, with short gilts too expensive while the longer-dated maturities will be supported by a spread over Bunds approaching 160 basis points," they said.
But with Brown balking at personal tax increases and rates set to rise, they said it was hard to see the budget as bullish for gilts.
Nonetheless, with Brown forecasting a public sector borrowing requirement of just 13.3 billion pounds this year, falling to 5.4 billion in 1998/99, gilts face few worries on the supply front.

"That means only a further 16.5 billion stg of gilts to sell (this year)," Adams said. "And the funding requirement would effectively disappear in 1998/99 were it not for the financing of redemptions."
To put that into context, in the last fiscal year, the Bank of England had to sell nearly 40 billion pounds of gilts to cover the PSBR and gilt redemptions.

Another budget bonus for gilts is the abolition of tax credits on Advance Corporation Tax, paid to pensions funds and the other large investment institutions, who were exempt from the tax. That removed a key tax incentive to buy British equities.

"The abolition of the ACT credit improves the return on gilts versus equities to UK pension funds, who dominate institutional investment in the UK," the Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said. "This may prompt some to make a strategic allocation out of equities into gilts."
Finally, with interest rates on the up and up, the pound will remain unhealthily strong and could soon break above three marks for the first time in six years.
It has already climbed by more than 20 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August, offering overseas investors a massive currency pick-up when holding gilts.
Yet 10-year gilts still yield more than 1.5 percentage points more than the equivalent German Bund.

"The gilt/Bund spread continues to suggest that international investors are being more than generously paid for holding gilts," said Adams at BZW. "We continue to look for a narrowing of the spread in the medium term and for weakness in Bunds to be the key driver."
